newsitem.title: USA: FBI says judgment errors made in Olympic bomb probe.
newsitem.headline: FBI says judgment errors made in Olympic bomb probe.

text.p: The U.S. Justice Department has found that FBI agents who interviewed Richard Jewell about last summer's Olympic bombing made a major error in judgment, FBI Director Louis Freeh said in a memo made available on Tuesday.

But Freeh said the Justice Department investigation found no evidence that FBI agents intentionally violated Jewell's civil rights or engaged in criminal misconduct during the controversial interview on the day he was named a suspect.

The April 1 memo by Freeh sought to allay what he called "concern" and "exaggerated rumours" circulating throughout the FBI about the proposed disciplinary measures for those agents involved in the interview of the former bombing suspect.
The FBI interviewed Jewell on July 30, three days after a pipe bomb packed with nails ripped through a crowd at an outdoor concert in Atlanta, leaving two people dead and more than 100 injured.

Jewell's attorneys have alleged agents tricked him into talking by saying they wanted his help in making a training film. Jewell claimed the FBI tried to get him to waive his constitutional rights as part of the ruse.
The Justice Department's Office of Professional Responsibility, the agency's internal watchdog unit, has conducted an internal probe into the handling of the Jewell interview.
"No one is claiming that the use of a ruse to encourage a suspect to talk is necessarily improper," Freeh said.
But he said there was a "major error in judgment" when warnings on the right to remain silent and to have a lawyer were "deceptively presented" as part of the training video.

"I can tell you that no prosecutor could go into court, and no director of the FBI could go before Congress, and claim that necessary constitutional warnings are adequately conveyed by telling a suspect that he is an actor in a training video and that he is being presented Miranda warnings (on silence rights) 'just like it's a real official interview'," he said.
Freeh said he himself made the judgment that Jewell should be given the warnings. But other FBI officials said Freeh did not know that it would be given as part of the training ruse.
Department officials said the probe's results will not be formally released until the FBI agents facing proposed disciplinary measures get a chance to respond.

The FBI has told five agents, including the head of its Atlanta office, a supervisor sent in from Kansas City and two agents who conducted the interview, they face possible measures ranging from a reprimand to 15-day suspension without pay.
The Freeh memo was first reported by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. It later was made available by Justice Department officials in Washington.

Jewell was working as a security guard at Centennial Olympic Park during an outdoor concert when he noticed the military-style backpack that contained the bomb. He reported the suspicious-looking package to police. The device then detonated as he helped clear concert-goers from the area.
Jewell initially was hailed as a hero. But he soon became the only named suspect in the investigation, though he was never charged with any crime.
After spending three months being hounded by the FBI and the news media, Jewell was publicly exonerated of any suspicion by the Justice Department.
